content.headline: Leaked files show Russia planned missile-launcher supply to Iran
content.shortHeadline: Leaked files show Russia planned missile launchers for Iran
content.standfirst: Documents reviewed by the Guardian describe a Russian order for 90 launchers, but do not show whether they were delivered. The disclosures offer a new glimpse of Moscow’s military ties with Tehran amid the Iran war.

image.caption: Vympel, the Russian company named in the leaked documents, designs missiles and launch systems.

sources.originalTitle: Russia agreed to supply Iran with 90 helicopter missile launchers

segments.body: A production schedule from Russian arms designer Vympel lists 90 launchers for the LMUR guided missile under an export contract that separate internal paperwork identifies as Iranian. The documents, obtained by Ukrainian private intelligence firm Dallas Analytics and shared with the Guardian, scheduled deliveries from late 2024 to December 2025. They do not establish whether the weapons arrived.

segments.title: What the documents add
segments.body: Russia has denied supplying military equipment to Iran for use in the current conflict. The Guardian says the documents provide fresh insight into military cooperation between the two countries, but the records do not establish whether the planned delivery went ahead. Vympel’s paperwork also described delays in key components that threatened production.

segments.title: Wider stakes
segments.body: The report comes as Washington weighs its next steps in the war. The Guardian says Russia has benefited from higher energy prices and the diversion of Western attention and military resources from Ukraine. European intelligence agencies have separately reported Russian support for Iran, including data and satellite imagery; Moscow’s role in the planned launcher supply remains unconfirmed.

content.headline: Bomb threats disrupt flights across Europe as officials urge caution on blame
content.shortHeadline: Bomb threats disrupt European flights; no devices found
content.standfirst: A wave of threats has diverted or delayed flights in several countries, including two flights from Copenhagen to Sofia. Authorities say searches found nothing suspicious; investigators have not identified a responsible group or state.

image.caption: An Aer Lingus plane at Évreux military airbase after a flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted following a bomb threat.

sources.originalTitle: Bomb threats disrupt at least 15 flights across Europe, raising hybrid war fears
Bomb threats on European flights: what do we know so far?

segments.body: At least 28 aircraft have faced security alerts or diversions this week, including at least 20 threats reported on Thursday, according to the Guardian’s explainer. All incidents have so far been confirmed as false alarms, with no suspicious items found. Ryanair was the most affected carrier, and airports in Sofia and Milan reported multiple incidents.

segments.title: No confirmed link
segments.body: Two Ryanair flights from Copenhagen and Madrid to Sofia made emergency landings in the Bulgarian capital; a London-to-Sofia flight was diverted to Plovdiv. A separate report says the alerts affected at least 15 flights on Thursday. The EU transport commissioner said it was too early to conclude that the incidents were linked, and no intelligence points to a particular group or state actor.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s explainer details how authorities in several countries reported negative searches and notes there is no clear pattern of airports or airlines targeted. It cautions that neither a coordinated campaign nor a state actor has been established.

segments.title: A costly response
segments.body: Airlines have little choice but to divert or land aircraft when a threat is judged credible, despite the expense and disruption. Aviation specialists say threats are assessed individually and that the response depends on whether the plane is on the ground or already in the air.

content.headline: Guinea-Bissau cancels disputed US-funded hepatitis B vaccine trial
content.shortHeadline: Guinea-Bissau cancels disputed newborn vaccine trial
content.standfirst: The proposed study would have withheld a hepatitis B vaccine from half of 14,000 newborns. Critics questioned its ethics; the Danish university involved says no babies were enrolled and no trial vaccinations took place.

image.caption: A baby receives a hepatitis B vaccination; the proposed study would have tested giving the dose at birth.

sources.originalTitle: Why a US-funded vaccine trial on babies was cancelled in Guinea-Bissau

segments.body: Guinea-Bissau has cancelled a proposed study of hepatitis B vaccination in newborns. The trial was designed to include 14,000 babies, with half receiving a dose shortly after birth and half not receiving it. The study had not begun: the University of Southern Denmark says no babies were enrolled and no vaccinations were given as research.

segments.title: Dispute over approval and ethics
segments.body: The World Health Organization’s representative in Guinea-Bissau said withholding a vaccine already recommended to protect newborns was unethical, especially where hepatitis B is widespread. The country’s health minister said the government’s suspension remained in force and he had not been informed of any approval to proceed. SDU said its own ethics committee had assessed the study positively, while stressing that separate authorisation from Guinea-Bissau was required.

segments.title: An unresolved police inquiry
segments.body: Guinea-Bissau’s Judicial Police searched the Bandim Health Project in October and seized a batch of vaccines. Police have not said whether the investigation concerns the proposed trial, the vaccine importation or other circumstances; the seizure alone does not establish that the vaccines were unsafe. The trial was funded by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

content.headline: Six people die in fire at residential building in Brooklyn
content.shortHeadline: Six dead after fire in Brooklyn residential building
content.standfirst: More than 230 emergency personnel responded to the early-morning blaze. Its cause is under investigation; officials have not established whether a lithium-ion battery found at the scene was connected.

image.caption: Fire and emergency medical crews responded to a residential-building fire in Brooklyn.

sources.originalTitle: Six dead and others injured in fire at New York City building

segments.body: Six people died after a fire engulfed the first and second floors of a residential building near Sunset Park in Brooklyn, New York, officials said. Four were pronounced dead at the scene; two others died in hospital. Six civilians were injured, including two critically, and three firefighters were also hurt.

More than 230 fire and emergency medical personnel were sent to the scene after the blaze was reported at about 01:40 local time on Thursday. The cause is being investigated. A hazardous-materials crew attended because a lithium-ion battery was present, but officials have not said whether it was linked to the fire.

content.headline: More than 250,000 join France strikes as unions demand higher wages
content.shortHeadline: France strikes draw more than 250,000, unions say
content.standfirst: Five unions joined students and other demonstrators in a national day of action over pay, living costs and public services. Disruption affected transport, schools and cultural sites, with clashes reported in Lyon and Rennes.

image.caption: CGT leader Sophie Binet said the protests had reached a new level of mobilisation.

sources.originalTitle: France holds new strikes and protests as unions demand immediate answers

segments.body: More than 250,000 people had joined protests in nearly 70 French towns and cities by 13:00 on Thursday, the CGT union said. Five unions organised the day of action, which grew out of protests over conditions and resources in high schools and broadened to include workers and demonstrators concerned about the cost of living.

segments.title: Disruption and demands
segments.body: The unions are seeking higher wages, including an increase in the minimum wage, and protection for public services. Disruption was reported in schools, hospitals and public transport; the Eiffel Tower and some rooms at the Louvre closed. The education ministry said 16% of teachers were on strike, while unions reported widespread disruption at schools and universities.

segments.title: Unrest in some cities
segments.body: The interior minister said 70,000 police were being deployed and promised a firm response to violence. Clashes were reported in Lyon and Rennes, including a car set alight in Lyon. The unions have also called for further protests and blockades on Friday and Saturday.

content.headline: Melania Trump hosts Russian and Ukrainian officials after ceasefire effort
content.shortHeadline: Melania Trump hosts Russian and Ukrainian delegations
content.standfirst: Ombudsmen and senior officials from Moscow and Kyiv are meeting at the White House after a ceasefire enabled evacuations from Russian-occupied Oleshky. The White House has not disclosed what Thursday’s meeting will cover.

image.caption: Melania Trump is hosting Russian and Ukrainian representatives at the White House.

sources.originalTitle: Melania Trump hosting Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House

segments.body: Russian and Ukrainian delegations are meeting at the White House on Thursday, hosted by US first lady Melania Trump. The delegations include the two countries’ human rights ombudsmen and senior officials who were involved in an evacuation mission from Oleshky, in the occupied Kherson region, after a ceasefire allowed several hundred people to leave.

segments.title: What remains unclear
segments.body: The White House says Melania Trump independently initiated engagement between the two sides and secured the ceasefire. Russian and Ukrainian officials have thanked her for brokering it, but neither has described the extent of her role. No details of the White House meeting have been released.

The meeting follows Ukraine’s award to Melania Trump of the Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, citing her humanitarian work. The BBC reports that US, Russian and Ukrainian representatives are also due to meet in Abu Dhabi next week for talks on postwar security and de-escalation.

content.headline: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison
content.shortHeadline: Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years under Hong Kong security law
content.standfirst: The pro-democracy activist, already imprisoned for nearly six years, pleaded guilty to colluding with foreign forces. Hong Kong and Chinese officials defended the ruling, while rights groups and the UK condemned it.

image.caption: Joshua Wong, the Hong Kong pro-democracy activist sentenced to 10 years in prison.

sources.originalTitle: Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years

segments.body: Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison for colluding with foreign forces under Hong Kong’s national security law. He had already spent nearly six years in prison and was due to be released in January. Two months and two days of the new term will run concurrently with his existing sentence, the judge said.

segments.title: A contested law
segments.body: Prosecutors said Wong and other campaigners lobbied for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing in 2020. Hong Kong’s chief executive and China’s foreign ministry defended the ruling as a matter of national security. The UK government called the sentence an example of the law being used against political expression; Human Rights Watch described it as cruel and unjust.

Wong’s sentence is the harshest imposed under the law on a pro-democracy activist, according to the BBC; the former media tycoon Jimmy Lai received a 20-year term. Critics say the security law has silenced dissent, while authorities argue it is needed to maintain stability.

content.headline: Democrats’ affordability promises face a veto and a divided Congress
content.shortHeadline: Can Democrats make life cheaper with Trump still able to veto?
content.standfirst: Democrats have pledged action on healthcare, tariffs, energy and housing after campaigning on the cost of living. But President Donald Trump can veto legislation, and the war’s effect on fuel prices is beyond their control.

image.caption: House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries says affordability will be a priority for his party.

sources.originalTitle: Food, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats actually make life cheaper?
What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress

segments.body: Democrats’ midterm victory was powered in part by voters’ concern over grocery, energy and fuel bills. The party says healthcare will be a priority, including restoring financial help for insurance and reversing Medicaid cuts. It also wants to change tariffs, build more homes and expand tax credits for families.

segments.title: Limits on what they can deliver
segments.body: Democrats will control Congress, but Trump remains president and can veto legislation. Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which the party does not have. Tariff changes and many other promises could therefore require Republican support or a deal with the White House.

segments.title: Bills may not fall quickly
segments.body: The BBC’s analysis notes that a possible compromise on healthcare subsidies and tax cuts may take until late 2027, with benefits arriving later. Fuel and fertiliser prices also depend on the Iran war. Democrats face an immediate test too: government funding runs out after 11 December, raising the prospect of another shutdown.

content.headline: Russell Brand convicted of rape and sexual assaults as police investigate two |
content.shortHeadline: Russell Brand convicted as police probe two further rape complaints
content.standfirst: A jury found the comedian guilty of one count of rape and three of sexual assault, and acquitted him of other charges. He is due to be sentenced on Monday; police say two further rape complaints remain under investigation.

image.caption: Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault after a trial at Southwark Crown Court.

sources.originalTitle: Russell Brand faces ‘significant’ jail term after being found guilty of rape
Russell Brand is being investigated over two new rape complaints, police say
Russell Brand kendt skyldig i voldtægt fra 2009
Kendt britisk komiker og skuespiller er skyldig i voldtægt
Misogyny and sexism of Russell Brand case have not gone away, TV insiders say

segments.body: Russell Brand was convicted at Southwark Crown Court of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. The jury acquitted him of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault. The judge said a significant custodial sentence was inevitable; Brand was remanded in custody until sentencing on Monday.

segments.title: Further investigation
segments.body: The Metropolitan Police said two further rape complaints against Brand remain under investigation and files have been sent to the Crown Prosecution Service. No charging decision on those complaints is reported. Brand was found guilty after a trial involving six women who gave evidence about allegations spanning 1999 to 2009.

segments.title: Questions for the industry
segments.body: The Guardian reports that informal concerns about Brand’s behaviour were not properly escalated or adequately addressed at some broadcasters and production companies. Former Channel 4 executive Alex Mahon said bad behaviour towards women had been tolerated in television for too long; industry figures say fear of career consequences can still deter people from speaking up.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s reporting adds testimony from former production staff who say earlier concerns about Brand were raised but went nowhere, and describes continuing fears that workers who complain may be sidelined.

content.headline: Bank of England raises rates to 4% as Iran war drives inflation fears
content.shortHeadline: Bank raises UK interest rate to 4% as inflation risks persist
content.standfirst: The first increase in more than three years will raise payments for some borrowers. Governor Andrew Bailey says another rise is possible if the Middle East conflict is not resolved, though the committee is divided on what should come next.

image.caption: The Bank of England’s rate-setting committee voted to raise the base rate to 4%.

sources.originalTitle: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%, the first increase for more than three years
Interest rates hiked to 4% in first increase in over three years
What does the UK interest rate rise mean for homeowners and savers?

segments.body: The Bank of England raised its base rate from 3.75% to 4%, with eight members of its Monetary Policy Committee voting for the move and one favouring a larger increase. The Bank said inflation, which was 3.5% in September, could rise to 4.9% by the middle of next year as higher energy costs feed through.

segments.title: Borrowers and savers
segments.body: The increase immediately affects about 510,000 tracker-mortgage holders, whose payments rise in line with the base rate; UK Finance estimates a typical monthly increase of about £31. Most fixed-rate borrowers will see no immediate change, though people whose deals are ending may face higher costs. Savings rates may rise, but banks are not required to pass on the full increase.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s consumer guide distinguishes the immediate effect on tracker mortgages from the delayed risk for fixed-rate borrowers, and notes that roughly 2.3 million fixed-rate deals are due to end in 2027.

segments.title: No settled path
segments.body: Governor Andrew Bailey said another increase is possible if the conflict in the Middle East continues, but stressed that the move should not be seen as the start of an inevitable series of hikes. Committee members differed: one described it as a one-off precaution, while others saw a case for further increases depending on inflation and energy prices.

content.headline: EU seeks stronger UK pledge on tuition fees ahead of reset summit
content.shortHeadline: EU presses UK for tuition-fee pledge before November summit
content.standfirst: Several EU states want a firmer commitment on discounted fees for European students before a 20 November meeting. The dispute could delay wider agreements on food trade and carbon markets; the UK government has not commented.

image.caption: A graduation ceremony at the University of Oxford.

sources.originalTitle: EU presses UK to guarantee discounted university tuition fees for European students
Tuition fees row threatens to derail Brexit reset… again

segments.body: The EU is pressing the UK to commit to lower university tuition fees for European students before a summit planned for 20 November. At least six member states opposed postponing the fees issue until after the meeting, according to EU sources cited by the Guardian. The UK government has been contacted for comment.

segments.title: A possible link to other deals
segments.body: The EU wants students from its member states to pay domestic rather than international rates, which can be several times higher. Some EU officials say the food and drink agreement and a deal linking emissions markets should not take effect without a satisfactory tuition-fee agreement. A proposed six-month delay to the fees talks has not secured sufficient support among member states.

perspectives.body: The i Paper reports that EU ambassadors rejected a draft compromise to delay negotiations by six months, while the UK has been concerned about the cost to cash-strapped universities.

segments.body: The planned summit is also expected to address youth exchanges and closer cooperation on strategic industries. The Guardian says the UK is prepared to spend up to £450m a year on discounted fees if it receives access to the EU’s Made in Europe industrial programme, but that programme will not be agreed at the November summit.

content.headline: Review proposes reducing England’s police forces to as few as nine
content.shortHeadline: Plan would merge England’s 39 police forces into regional services
content.standfirst: A review awaiting publication proposes replacing most forces in England and Wales with larger regional organisations. Some police leaders support radical consolidation; others question the evidence and warn that forces could become too remote from local communities.

image.caption: The proposed regional forces would sit above local policing units.

sources.originalTitle: Police chiefs divided on proposal to axe England’s 39 forces to create ‘super forces’

segments.body: A government-commissioned review by former Metropolitan Police commissioner Bernard Hogan-Howe proposes cutting England’s 39 forces to between nine and 18 regional forces, with a separate force for Wales, according to the Guardian. The report has been sent to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood and is expected to be published before Christmas.

segments.title: Scale versus local accountability
segments.body: Supporters say larger forces could respond faster to new threats and pool costly back-office work. The proposed structure would retain more than 150 local policing units for neighbourhood work, with a national force focused on counter-terrorism and serious organised crime. Some chief constables and other police leaders oppose or question the scale of the mergers.

segments.title: Concerns over evidence and delay
segments.body: Critics say very large forces could weaken local knowledge and point to failures at some of the country’s largest forces. One chief constable warned that the financial return could take five or six years; another questioned whether bigger forces perform better. The government has not published the review, and the timetable for a white paper is in the new year.

content.headline: Middlesbrough youth joblessness highlights barriers beyond training
content.shortHeadline: Middlesbrough’s young jobseekers face scarce work and poor transport
content.standfirst: One in six local people aged 16 to 25 are not in education, employment or training, as young residents and job coaches describe limited vacancies and unreliable links to nearby cities. The government is preparing a national review of youth unemployment.

image.caption: A youth employment hub in Middlesbrough, where jobseekers face barriers including scarce vacancies and transport.

sources.originalTitle: Inside the hardest place to be young in England, where one in six under-25s are jobless

segments.body: In Middlesbrough, 17% of people aged 16 to 25 are not in education, employment or training, according to figures cited by the i Paper. Young jobseeker James says he has applied for many jobs, while friends who left for university in Liverpool found work quickly. Locally, he says, openings are often in hospitality or warehouse work.

segments.title: Transport and a changing economy
segments.body: Job-centre staff say infrequent and frequently cancelled trains, and limited bus services, make it harder for young people to reach work in Newcastle and elsewhere. The closure of major industrial employment in nearby Billingham was described by local staff as an economic shock; the disappearance of those jobs and spending has also reduced entry-level work in the town centre.

The report describes James taking part in a government work-experience scheme and job-centre staff connecting young people with employers. But local workers say there is no single solution, and point to a national shortage of entry-level roles: a Work Foundation report cited by the i Paper found one starter job for every three young people seeking work.

content.headline: Poundland owners pressed to protect jobs as sale talks continue
content.shortHeadline: Government presses Poundland owners to protect 11,000 jobs
content.standfirst: The retailer has filed a notice to appoint administrators, while potential buyers consider offers for the chain and its stores. The government says the owners have committed to prioritising bids that protect UK jobs.

image.caption: Poundland filed a notice to appoint administrators last week.

sources.originalTitle: Government holds crunch talks over future of Poundland

segments.body: Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has held talks with US-based owners Gordon Brothers, who have committed to prioritising bids that protect UK jobs, according to a source cited by the i Paper. Poundland filed a notice to appoint administrators last week, putting around 11,000 jobs at risk.

segments.title: Sale options remain open
segments.body: Gordon Brothers began a sale process in September. The i Paper reports that advisers are assessing an offer from investment group Xyra, while Tesco, Poundstretcher owner Fortress and other retailers have discussed buying some stores. No buyer or final deal has been announced.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has urged the owners to find a practical solution that keeps viable stores open. Downing Street has criticised their handling of the sale process, saying the government wants an explanation for why no offer to keep the company going has been accepted.

content.headline: Mould in rented homes linked to health concerns as quick fixes questioned
content.shortHeadline: Renters describe mould and health concerns as quick fixes fail
content.standfirst: A tenant’s long-running dispute with her council illustrates wider concerns about damp in rented homes. Experts say cosmetic cleaning may leave underlying moisture problems unresolved, while the precise health effects of mould exposure remain an area of ongoing research.

image.caption: The report examines landlords’ use of quick-fix firms to treat damp and mould.

sources.originalTitle: ‘My home is so mouldy it’s rotting’: The renters living in dangerously damp homes

segments.body: Ellen Rashbrook says mould and leaks in her council-owned flat in Putney were followed by years of health problems. A doctor wrote in 2024 that mould was highly likely to be a major factor in her poor health. The council declined to comment on her case because legal proceedings are ongoing; its expert witness says only minor work is needed, a view disputed by Rashbrook’s expert.

segments.title: A wider housing problem
segments.body: The i Paper cites an English Housing Survey estimate that 1.4 million homes had a damp problem, most of them rented, and says an estimated 142,000 homes had the most serious Category 1 hazard. Experts and campaigners warn that cleaning visible mould without fixing the underlying moisture may not solve the problem.

The article reports that new requirements for landlords to investigate damp and mould complaints may encourage some to use quick, cosmetic treatments. Medical experts say more research is needed to understand the full range of possible health effects; the exact impacts of mould exposure are not settled science.

content.headline: Læsø care home still has patient-safety deficiencies, new order says
content.shortHeadline: Læsø care home still lacks key patient records, watchdog finds
content.standfirst: A fresh inspection found missing information on residents’ illnesses and medication. The local committee chair says improvements have been made but the home is not yet where it needs to be; an earlier inspection found care itself was good.

image.caption: Læsø Municipality allocated extra funding to the care home earlier this year.

sources.originalTitle: Omdiskuteret plejehjem har stadig ikke styr på patientsikkerheden

segments.body: Denmark’s Patient Safety Authority has issued a new order to Læsø Care Home after a 22 September inspection found significant gaps in residents’ records, including information about illnesses and medication. The authority says the deficiencies affect patient safety.

segments.title: Changes not yet complete
segments.body: Care and health committee chair Michael Møller Kristensen said he was not surprised by the order, following severe criticism in an earlier report. He said the municipality has made progress but is not yet at its goal. An elder-care inspection found the care itself was good, he said, but patient safety must also be in order.

The municipality allocated an additional 1.5 million kroner to the care home earlier this year, including for more nurses and internal restructuring. Responsibility for nursing care had previously been moved from the home to the municipality’s home-care service after the earlier safety findings.

content.headline: Maersk posts 22bn kroner profit but shares fall as analysts expect more
content.shortHeadline: Maersk profit reaches 22bn kroner; shares fall on expectations
content.standfirst: Chief executive Vincent Clerc called the third-quarter result exceptionally strong and raised the company’s annual outlook. Analysts questioned how long high freight rates and port delays can sustain earnings; the share price fell sharply.

image.caption: Maersk chief executive Vincent Clerc presented the company’s third-quarter results.

sources.originalTitle: Mærsk-aktien faldt ti procent: Direktøren revser analytikere

segments.body: A.P. Møller-Mærsk reported an operating profit of 22 billion kroner for July to September. Chief executive Vincent Clerc called it one of the company’s strongest quarterly results outside the pandemic years and raised its full-year earnings expectation to more than 50 billion kroner.

segments.title: Why investors remain cautious
segments.body: The company’s shares fell by more than 10% at the opening of trading and were down about 8% around midday, according to DR. Analyst Haider Anjum said earnings are supported by port congestion, high spot rates and disruptions, and questioned how long those conditions will last. Maersk expects the market to remain similarly strong in the fourth quarter.

Disruption in the Middle East has led many ships to sail around Africa rather than use the Suez Canal, while delays at ports have reduced available shipping capacity. Maersk has been able to operate full ships and charge higher prices, but the company’s outlook depends on how long those pressures persist.

content.headline: Bestseller owner buys Aarhus Airport buildings and land for 90m kroner
content.shortHeadline: Heartland buys Aarhus Airport property for 90m kroner
content.standfirst: The sale-and-leaseback deal is intended to ease pressure on the airport’s finances, but Heartland will not take over operations. The three owner municipalities remain responsible for running and developing the airport.

image.caption: Anders Holch Povlsen’s company Heartland is buying property at Aarhus Airport.

sources.originalTitle: Bestseller-ejer køber Aarhus Lufthavn

segments.body: Heartland, the company behind Bestseller owner Anders Holch Povlsen, is buying Aarhus Airport’s buildings and land for 90 million kroner. The deal covers the terminal, hotel, parking areas and part of the site. Aarhus Airport will continue operating the airport and will lease the property from Heartland.

segments.title: Debt and ownership
segments.body: Aarhus Airport has struggled financially for years. As part of the deal, an earlier 200-million-kroner loan from Aarhus Municipality and about 90 million kroner in accrued interest will be converted into share capital rather than repaid. The municipality will sell shares to Syddjurs and Norddjurs to maintain the agreed ownership proportions.

Aarhus Municipality will own 90% of the airport company, with Syddjurs and Norddjurs together holding 10%. The municipalities retain responsibility for airport operations and development; the property transaction is intended to free up resources and support investment, including completion of an ongoing terminal expansion.

content.headline: Danish teenagers charged in alleged online sexual abuse linked to 1414 network
content.shortHeadline: Two teenagers charged in alleged abuse linked to 1414 network
content.standfirst: Police say the boys pressured a girl under 12 to harm herself sexually and shared a video. The teenagers deny the allegations; the investigation is still ongoing, and no charges have been brought against one of them beyond the existing case.

image.caption: Graphic accompanying DR’s investigation into the 1414 online network.

sources.originalTitle: Drenge med tilknytning til det sadistiske online-netværk 1414 sigtet for digital voldtægt

segments.body: Two Danish boys, aged 16 and 17 at the time of the alleged events, have been charged with offences including digital rape after allegedly pressuring a girl under 12 to harm herself sexually and filming and sharing the video. The alleged conduct took place over 10 months from December 2024, according to a charge document obtained by DR.

segments.title: Reported links and denials
segments.body: DR reports that usernames associated with two leaders of the sadistic online network 1414 match names used by the accused, and says several independent sources connected the case to the network. Europol confirmed to DR that 1414 was founded and led by two Danish youths. One defence lawyer disputes the assumptions linking a client to a network username; both defendants have denied the charges.

segments.title: Investigation continues
segments.body: More than a year after the boys were charged, the case remains under investigation. West Copenhagen Police confirmed the delay but declined to explain it or give details of progress. DR says its monitoring of online groups found a profile using one of the usernames active in other groups; its reporting does not establish that this activity proves the defendants’ involvement.

content.headline: Middelfart school staff record 1,919 alleged abusive incidents in two weeks
content.shortHeadline: Middelfart school logs 1,919 abusive incidents in two weeks
content.standfirst: A municipal spot-check recorded threats, insults and physical incidents against staff in a special-needs department. The school committee chair says a report due on 17 November will examine the causes; the municipality says its current measures have not yet shown measurable results.

sources.originalTitle: Ansatte på skole registrerede krænkelser 1919 gange på to uger

segments.body: Staff at the full-day department of Østre School in Middelfart recorded 1,919 incidents described as abusive over two weeks in September, according to figures obtained by TV 2 Fyn. The records included 1,573 cases of abusive language, 77 threats, and incidents involving spitting or biting, scratching, and hitting or kicking.

segments.title: Staff turnover and response
segments.body: The figures also show 55 approved uses of restraint on pupils at the department from January to October. A former school-board chair said 20 employees had started and left the department in the same year, leaving just two staff members with more than a year’s service. The municipality says it has strengthened staffing and risk assessments, but the effect is not yet measurable.

The school committee chair said the figures are high but reflect the needs of pupils in the specialist provision, and that there is no quick fix. An external analysis is due on 17 November. The acting department head and municipal school chief declined TV 2 Fyn’s interview requests.

content.headline: Why checking your coat can now cost £15 on a night out
content.shortHeadline: Why club cloakrooms can cost £15
content.standfirst: Bag storage at some UK venues now costs more than £13. Rising operating costs and post-2017 security measures help explain the increase—but clubbers say the price and quality of storage can be hard to accept.

image.caption: Lockers at Drumsheds in London.

sources.originalTitle: Once it was a £1 hanger. Now it’s a £15 locker. Why do cloakrooms cost so much on a night out?

segments.body: The price of putting a coat or bag into storage has climbed sharply at some UK venues. The Guardian reports charges of up to £15 for a large bag at Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena, and up to £13.20 at London club Drumsheds. Average spending per person on a night out has also risen, from £20.95 in 2020 to £28.06 in 2026, according to the Night Time Industries Association.

segments.title: Security, staffing and the experience
segments.body: The article links the spread of off-site storage to security requirements introduced after the 2017 Manchester Arena attack and to venues’ difficulties staffing traditional cloakrooms. Some customers describe paying for storage in places they felt were neither secure nor fit for purpose. Others, including the manager of Edinburgh’s Carpet Shop, argue that a low-cost, staffed cloakroom is part of the club experience.

content.headline: Can music help turn climate grief into action? Flow is making the case
content.shortHeadline: Flow brings music and climate action together
content.standfirst: The Flow collective has brought together women artists from several countries for an album about water, with Charlotte Church and Maxine Peake among its contributors. The project hopes to bring music into the climate conversation at Cop31.

image.caption: Charlotte Church, a contributor to the Flow project.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Music is the most powerful way of connecting to what’s happening’: can this album change your mind about the climate crisis?

segments.body: Flow began with musicians meeting online and has grown into an album co-produced by Jennifer Decilveo, featuring artists including Charlotte Church, Maxine Peake and Nadine Shah. The collective will take part in an event at Cop31 in Turkey. Project manager Nikita Llerena says art can reach emotional dimensions of the climate debate that data alone cannot.

segments.title: Whose voices are heard?
segments.body: The album and its accompanying documentary focus on water and women’s experiences of the climate crisis. Indigenous teacher Márcia Mura describes how floods, droughts, dams and pollution have changed the Madeira River, and stresses that Indigenous women must speak for themselves. She helped establish the Mura Collective to connect women defending local waters.

content.headline: Manic Street Preachers revisit the weight of The Holy Bible
content.shortHeadline: The Manics reckon with The Holy Bible’s legacy
content.standfirst: A new live recording documents the band performing their stark 1994 album in full. James Dean Bradfield reflects on the words of missing bandmate Richey Edwards, the strain of revisiting them and what the record still means.

image.caption: Manic Street Preachers: Nicky Wire, James Dean Bradfield and Sean Moore.

sources.originalTitle: Manic Street Preachers: ‘We just weren’t equipped to deal with Richey’s problems’

segments.body: The Holy Bible Live captures Manic Street Preachers playing their 1994 album at London’s Roundhouse in 2014. The record’s lyrics, written chiefly by Richey Edwards, confront subjects including mental illness, atrocity and political violence. Edwards disappeared in 1995 and was legally declared dead in 2008; his absence, Bradfield says, remains part of the band’s history.

segments.title: A difficult reckoning
segments.body: Bradfield describes the anniversary concerts as a physical and emotional challenge. Some lines were difficult to sing, and memories of Edwards’ distress returned during performances. He says the band did not know how to respond to Edwards’ mental health crisis at the time, and questions whether they should have stopped him touring. The live album, he says, records a connection with the work that the band is proud of.

content.headline: Richard Thompson looks back at Fairport Convention’s tragedy and his new album
content.shortHeadline: Richard Thompson on loss, memory and new songs
content.standfirst: The folk musician discusses his 20th solo album, his early years in London and the 1969 crash that killed Fairport Convention drummer Martin Lamble and Thompson’s girlfriend, Jeannie Franklyn.

image.caption: Richard Thompson.

sources.originalTitle: Fairport Convention’s Richard Thompson on the crash that killed his bandmate

segments.body: Richard Thompson’s new record, Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, is the latest release in a six-decade career. In conversation with the i Paper, he looks back on Fairport Convention’s beginnings and the London music scene of the 1960s, while describing his ongoing interest in making music that does not sound overly American—even though he has lived in the United States for much of the past 35 years.

segments.title: The loss that stayed with him
segments.body: Thompson also reflects on a 1969 road accident that killed Lamble, aged 19, and Franklyn. He says the band did not know how to deal with the loss and tried to carry on by making Liege and Lief. Looking back through his memoir, he says, prompted him to revisit memories he had shut away; some of his new songs draw on people and experiences from his past.

content.headline: Rita Wilson’s new album gives voice to women’s lives and changing bodies
content.shortHeadline: Rita Wilson on finding her voice in music
content.standfirst: On Sound of a Woman, the actor and songwriter traces love, loss, ageing and self-acceptance. She also discusses Hollywood’s ageism and why songwriting gave her room to express what some acting roles did not.

image.caption: Rita Wilson.

sources.originalTitle: Rita Wilson: ‘My body turned on me – but it was also there to heal me’

segments.body: Rita Wilson describes Sound of a Woman as a set of songs about the different experiences women have across their lives, from young love to ageing and loss. The album includes songs about female friendship, body image and illness. Wilson says “Whose Body Is This?” reflects acceptance of what her body has endured, including a bilateral mastectomy after her breast cancer diagnosis in 2015.

segments.title: A second creative life
segments.body: Wilson says she turned more seriously to music in her 50s after feeling creatively stuck in acting roles that often cast her as a nurturing mother or friend. Writing songs, she says, let her speak in ways those parts had not. She also calls the entertainment business ageist and says she had once been afraid to say so publicly.

content.headline: Bernie Taupin steps out on his own with a new solo album
content.shortHeadline: Bernie Taupin makes a solo album on his own terms
content.standfirst: The lyricist behind many of Elton John’s best-known songs says he relishes anonymity. At 76, he has written both lyrics and music for The Sea Has No Mercy, a reflective album he describes as a late-life manifesto.

image.caption: Bernie Taupin.

sources.originalTitle: ‘At my age, I can rant!’ Bernie Taupin on Elton John, hellraising vampires and competing in full-blown rodeos

segments.body: Bernie Taupin says he enjoys being recognised only when people see his name on a credit card. Best known for his long songwriting partnership with Elton John, he has released The Sea Has No Mercy, an album on which he wrote both the lyrics and the music. The Guardian describes it as a dark mix of folk, country and ambient textures, with Taupin’s voice carrying a reflective, sometimes grouchy tone.

segments.title: Writing beyond the partnership
segments.body: Taupin says he wanted to make something “100% selfish” after writing his autobiography. He also reflects on the Hollywood Vampires, his life in the United States and the way lyrics can change meaning when Elton John sings them. He plans to make another album and has a career-spanning documentary due later this year.

content.headline: Twisted Teens find tenderness beneath the noise on The Holy Cross Tigers
content.shortHeadline: Twisted Teens balance garage-rock rush with melancholy
content.standfirst: The New Orleans band’s third album of 2026 shifts between rough-edged rock, tape experiments and moments of quiet reflection. Pitchfork hears breakup songs that stay lively without hiding their hurt.

sources.originalTitle: The Holy Cross Tigers

segments.body: The Holy Cross Tigers mixes distorted garage-rock energy with drum machines, synth loops and abrupt breaks that interrupt the rush of the songs. Pitchfork hears a band drawing on rock history without settling into straightforward revivalism, as singer Caspian Hollywell’s storytelling and the group’s strange sonic turns add mystery to the familiar scruffy surface.

segments.title: A party with a darker edge
segments.body: The album is described as a breakup record, but it does not become a subdued lament. The review finds Hollywell balancing merriment and melancholy, with songs that turn to nature for images of renewal and tracks that bring in spoken word and dub-like textures. The result is an album of infectious tunes that also makes space for grief and change.

content.headline: Yeah Yeah Yeahs recast their catalogue with strings on a live album
content.shortHeadline: Yeah Yeah Yeahs reveal the vulnerability in their songs
content.standfirst: On Hidden in Pieces, the New York trio reshapes songs from across its career in intimate arrangements, often with strings and organ. Pitchfork finds warmth and emotional force in the quieter setting, though some of the originals’ bite is lost.

sources.originalTitle: Hidden in Pieces: Live at the Royal Albert Hall

segments.body: Recorded during the band’s 25th-anniversary tour at London’s Royal Albert Hall, Hidden in Pieces brings older songs into more intimate arrangements, with strings, piano and the hall’s organ. Pitchfork argues that the gentler performances make the songwriting’s ache and vulnerability more audible, and singles out Karen O’s shifting, imperfect vocals as a particular strength.

segments.title: What the new arrangements change
segments.body: The review describes “Maps” as a moment of shared emotion when the audience takes over the chorus, and finds new weight in material from Cool It Down. But the stripped-back “Warrior” and “Zero” lose some of their original tension and dancefloor force. The album’s warmth, the review suggests, is not a substitute for the volatility of the band’s earlier sound.

content.headline: One in a Million follows a Syrian family across ten years of change
content.shortHeadline: A decade with one Syrian family, from flight to home
content.standfirst: Filmmakers Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes began following Israa’s family as they fled Syria in 2015. Their documentary continues through the family’s new life in Germany and Israa’s journey into adulthood.

image.caption: Israa and her father, Tarek, in One in a Million.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Children were wearing fake life jackets’: one Syrian family’s terrifying, 10-year journey

segments.body: Azzam and MacInnes first met Israa, then 11, in İzmir as she and her family prepared to cross from Turkey to Greece. They continued filming after the family reached Germany. Their documentary, One in a Million, follows Israa from childhood into her early 20s, turning a film about flight and resettlement into a longer account of growing up and family life.

segments.title: A relationship beyond the camera
segments.body: The filmmakers describe becoming close to the family as they travelled with them, while also pausing filming when Israa disclosed that her father had been hitting her. Now a mother of two and training for local government work, Israa says she trusted Azzam from their first meeting. Watching the crossing as an adult, she says, made clear how dangerous it had been.

content.headline: Being Heumann tells the story of a pivotal disability rights campaign
content.shortHeadline: Judy Heumann’s fight for disability rights on screen
content.standfirst: Ruth Madeley plays activist Judy Heumann in a drama about the 1977 San Francisco sit-in that helped secure federal accessibility protections. The film brings a landmark campaign to the screen, though it softens part of the government’s response.

image.caption: Ruth Madeley as Judy Heumann in Being Heumann.

sources.originalTitle: Being Heumann review – stirring biopic of a pioneering disability rights campaigner

segments.body: Being Heumann follows disability rights campaigner Judy Heumann, played by Ruth Madeley, a disabled actor and activist. The film depicts the 1977 occupation of federal offices in San Francisco, where Heumann and a coalition including gay rights groups and the Black Panthers pressed for the government to implement accessibility provisions in the Rehabilitation Act.

segments.title: A coalition and its compromises
segments.body: The Guardian praises the film’s energetic ensemble and its attention to debates within the protest group, as well as its frankness about disabled people’s sexuality. The review also notes a significant omission: the film does not clearly show that officials authorised efforts to starve the protesters out before the government conceded.

content.headline: La Bola Negra traces queer lives and erased histories across Spain
content.shortHeadline: La Bola Negra connects queer lives across generations
content.standfirst: This Spanish film links three men’s stories in 1932, 1939 and 2017, exploring desire, exclusion and inherited trauma. The Guardian praises its performances and visual craft while noting that explanation sometimes diminishes its mystery.

image.caption: Álvaro Lafuente Calvo in La Bola Negra.

sources.originalTitle: La Bola Negra review – the complicated secrets of gay sexuality in Spain are brilliantly told

segments.body: La Bola Negra connects three stories from different periods of Spanish life: a man rejected by an elite club over rumours about his sexuality, a soldier who falls in love with a Republican prisoner, and a contemporary student researching queer identities. The film draws on Federico García Lorca and considers how gay lives and histories have been concealed or denied.

segments.title: Mystery, memory and desire
segments.body: The Guardian praises the performances and the film’s careful visual construction, including its shifts between the three eras. It finds the story rewarding but argues that spelling out the connection between the narratives takes away some of the mystery and poetry that initially give the film its force.

content.headline: Renate Reinsve on the role that nearly came after she quit acting
content.shortHeadline: Renate Reinsve on the role that changed her career
content.standfirst: Reinsve was considering leaving acting when Joachim Trier offered her the lead in The Worst Person in the World. She tells the BBC how the film changed her life and why she was drawn to a very different role in Fjord.

sources.originalTitle: 'It stopped me quitting acting': The Norwegian star on her life-changing role in 2021's The Worst Person in the World

segments.body: Renate Reinsve says she thought her Cannes appearance for The Worst Person in the World would be her first and last red carpet: she had been considering a different career after struggling to find film work. Director Joachim Trier called with the lead role the day after she decided to quit. The film’s success changed the course of her career.

segments.title: A different kind of performance
segments.body: In Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord, Reinsve plays Lisbet, a quiet evangelical mother whose children are removed amid suspicions of abuse. Reinsve says she was interested in finding compassion for a character unlike herself. She also agrees with Mungiu that the film should invite audiences to question their assumptions rather than instruct them what to think.

content.headline: I Play Rocky turns Stallone’s breakthrough into a Hollywood underdog story
content.shortHeadline: I Play Rocky makes a spirited story of Stallone’s rise
content.standfirst: Anthony Ippolito plays Sylvester Stallone in a brisk drama about the making of Rocky and the unknown writer’s insistence on playing its lead. The Guardian finds the film entertaining and more mythic than the original.

image.caption: Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone in I Play Rocky.

sources.originalTitle: I Play Rocky review – Anthony Ippolito adds knockout sweetness to the story of Stallone’s Hollywood triumph

segments.body: I Play Rocky follows Stallone as a struggling actor who wrote the screenplay for Rocky and refused offers to sell it unless he could play the lead. The Guardian describes the film as an enjoyable, fast-moving account of the decision and the obstacles around making the 1976 boxing drama.

segments.title: More than an imitation
segments.body: Anthony Ippolito is a striking physical and vocal likeness of the young Stallone, the review says, but also brings warmth and humour to the role. The film’s central appeal is its Hollywood story of self-belief and success—one the reviewer finds even more mythic than Rocky itself.

content.headline: Jimmy gives James Stewart’s life a too-neat wartime arc
content.shortHeadline: Jimmy’s James Stewart story is too neatly arranged
content.standfirst: KJ Apa captures some of Stewart’s voice and physical mannerisms in a biopic focused on his wartime service. The Guardian finds the performance more convincing than a film that narrows the actor’s complicated career into a simple lesson.

image.caption: KJ Apa in Jimmy.

sources.originalTitle: Jimmy review – simple-minded James Stewart biopic is too straightforward

segments.body: Jimmy focuses on James Stewart’s decision to serve in the second world war, his experience as a bomber pilot and his return to Hollywood. KJ Apa gives a surprisingly assured impression of Stewart’s distinctive voice and gangly physicality, the Guardian says.

segments.title: A life narrowed to one theme
segments.body: The review argues that the film makes Stewart’s artistic career secondary to a tidy account of wartime trauma and recovery, leaving little room for the more complicated parts of his later work or personal life. Apa’s performance, it concludes, cannot overcome the biopic’s schematic storytelling.

content.headline: Think of England turns a dubious wartime premise into a grim misfire
content.shortHeadline: Think of England is a serious misfire
content.standfirst: Richard Hawkins’s film imagines the British government commissioning porn for troops during the second world war. The Guardian says its uncertain historical basis and awkward handling of sexual violence, trauma and misogyny undermine the story.

image.caption: Natalie Quarry and Ollie Maddigan in Think of England.

sources.originalTitle: Think of England review – far-fetched tale of state-sponsored second world war porn turns deadly serious

segments.body: Think of England imagines a group assembled in the Orkneys to make a pornographic film for British troops. The Guardian notes that the premise is presented as an urban myth, but finds no clear evidence for the claimed wartime commission beyond online material connected to the film. Britain’s Political Warfare Executive is known to have dropped pornographic leaflets over Germany, a different undertaking.

segments.title: A tonal and historical problem
segments.body: The review says the film appears to promise a saucy comedy but becomes a grave drama about sexual violence, PTSD and misogyny without addressing those subjects convincingly. It singles out one scene about an actor learning to perform for the camera, but finds the rest increasingly implausible and jarring.

content.headline: Raise the Red Lantern remains a ruthless study of power and survival
content.shortHeadline: Raise the Red Lantern’s intimate politics endure
content.standfirst: Zhang Yimou’s 1991 film follows Gong Li’s young bride through the rivalries and rituals of a wealthy household. The Guardian revisits a tightly controlled drama whose domestic world becomes a study of power and survival.

image.caption: Gong Li in Raise the Red Lantern.

sources.originalTitle: Raise the Red Lantern review – Gong Li gives a decade-defining performance in an addictively ruthless masterpiece

segments.body: Gong Li plays Songlian, a university student who becomes the fourth mistress in a wealthy man’s household in 1920s China. The family’s strict rituals, including the nightly choice of which mistress receives the red lanterns, shape a world of privilege, rivalry and carefully managed humiliation.

segments.title: Ritual as power
segments.body: The Guardian describes the film as a study of women forced to compete for security and status within a system that treats them as possessions. Its enclosed setting makes each gesture and rule feel inescapable, as Songlian learns to anticipate plots and punishments while trying to survive.

content.headline: Channel 4 axes Married at First Sight UK after misconduct allegations
content.shortHeadline: Married at First Sight UK is cancelled
content.standfirst: Channel 4 has ended the reality series after reviews followed allegations by three women connected to filming. The broadcaster says it will not air the series made during the review; the reviews did not investigate the allegations themselves.

image.caption: Channel 4’s headquarters in London.

sources.originalTitle: Channel 4 axes Married at First Sight UK after rape allegations

segments.body: Channel 4 has cancelled Married at First Sight UK after two women alleged rape during filming and a third alleged sexual misconduct. The broadcaster also says it will not show the sixth series, which was in production before stronger safeguards were recommended, or resume work on its planned spin-off.

segments.title: What the reviews did—and did not—find
segments.body: A review of current safeguards said the programme could continue with changes, but Channel 4 chief executive Priya Dogra said applying the recommendations would fundamentally alter the format. A separate law-firm review of the protocols in place at the time found isolated failures to implement them, but no breach of the Ofcom code on the evidence available. It was not asked to examine the allegations.

segments.title: A contributor’s lawyer raises concerns
segments.body: Lia Perin, who represents a contributor whose allegation appeared on Panorama, says the review findings raise further questions. She points to concerns about pressure for contestants to be intimate and says risks built into the format should have been addressed earlier.

content.headline: Black Doves returns with spies, hitmen and a friendship worth watching
content.shortHeadline: Black Doves finds feeling amid the mayhem
content.standfirst: Keira Knightley, Ben Whishaw and Sarah Lancashire anchor a second season full of implausible plots and relentless violence. The Guardian says the show’s real draw is the characters’ friendship and the cast’s chemistry.

image.caption: Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw in Black Doves.

sources.originalTitle: Black Doves review – Ben Whishaw, Keira Knightley and Sarah Lancashire are spine-tinglingly good

segments.body: In the second season, Helen Webb is newly installed in No 10 while her handler, Reed, has disappeared. Helen turns to hitman Sam and his associates for help, even as an MI5 officer begins to notice gaps in her backstory. The Guardian calls the plotting wildly implausible, but praises the performances of Knightley, Whishaw and Lancashire.

segments.title: The bond beneath the body count
segments.body: The review finds little jeopardy in a world where the leads repeatedly escape consequences, but argues that the relationship between Helen and Sam gives the series its emotional core. Their friendship, wry banter and shared sense of life’s bleakness offer moments of poignancy amid the gunfights and conspiracies.

content.headline: Stick’s second season sends Owen Wilson’s golf pro back on the road
content.shortHeadline: Stick lets Owen Wilson chase one more golf dream
content.standfirst: Pryce Cahill is back coaching his young protégé and pursuing a late-career comeback. The Guardian finds the comedy’s relaxed warmth strengthened by its reflections on family, regret and the choices that cannot be undone.

image.caption: Rhea Seehorn and Owen Wilson in Stick.

sources.originalTitle: Stick review – you really need Owen Wilson’s beautiful golf comedy in your life

segments.body: Season two finds Pryce Cahill trying to give 17-year-old golfer Santi room to make his own decisions as the professional tour beckons. Pryce, meanwhile, decides to return to competition and set his sights on winning the US Open at 55. The Guardian praises Owen Wilson’s easy charm and the show’s appealing ensemble.

segments.title: More than a sports comedy
segments.body: The review says the series’ easygoing tone sits alongside a deeper story about fatherhood and loss. Pryce’s past, including the death of his young son, colours his advice to Santi and gives the show its melancholy edge. As the young golfer grows more independent, Pryce must learn when to step back.

content.headline: Tall Tales and Murder races through a crowded Irish crime story
content.shortHeadline: Tall Tales and Murder is lively but overstuffed
content.standfirst: The adaptation of Caimh McDonnell’s Dublin Trilogy moves from a care home to a gangland feud over buried treasure. The Guardian enjoys its pace and cast but finds the many plots and tonal shifts hard to follow.

image.caption: Ella Lily Hyland, Aidan Gillen and Casey Walsh in Tall Tales and Murder.

sources.originalTitle: Tall Tales and Murder review – this Irish version of The Wire makes for mile-a-minute TV

segments.body: Tall Tales and Murder follows care-home worker Bridget and local miscreant Paul as a man emerging from a coma revives an underworld dispute over Celtic gold. The series also takes in romance, crime, a dysfunctional care home and multiple side stories. The Guardian says there is plenty to keep the pace lively, but that the show’s many strands can leave viewers confused.

segments.title: Good parts lost in the sprawl
segments.body: The review singles out the chemistry between Ella Lily Hyland and Casey Walsh, Sheila Flitton’s performance as a dementia patient, and the careful handling of one character’s childhood abuse. But it argues that the gangland plot grows overwrought and that some early stories and characters are left behind without resolution.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors finale delivers a late turn after a rocky run
content.shortHeadline: The Celebrity Traitors ends with a surprise Faithful win
content.standfirst: The finale sends the remaining Traitors home and awards £83,000 to the Faithfuls’ charities. Two i Paper writers see a welcome late reversal, while also questioning the chaotic setup and James Acaster’s early recruitment.

image.caption: The Celebrity Traitors’ final round table.

sources.originalTitle: One player’s lack of ego saved Celebrity Traitors
James Acaster was stitched up

segments.body: The final mission and round table bring a series of turns: Maya Jama is banished, then Sebastian challenges Kenny’s decision to end the game and helps persuade Romesh Ranganathan to change his vote. Kenny is exposed as the final Traitor, leaving £83,000 for the Faithfuls’ charities. The i Paper’s finale review credits Sebastian’s lack of ego with helping produce the upset.

segments.title: A finale shaped by the opening episodes
segments.body: A separate i Paper account argues that the season’s instability began early: Richard E Grant’s accidental confession led to his quick exit, while James Acaster was recruited before he had the usual opportunity to decline. The writer says the rapid turnover of Traitors and Acaster’s discomfort made the game feel disjointed well before the finale.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s analysis focuses on how the rules and early recruitment choices put pressure on Acaster and shaped the season’s uneven trajectory.

content.headline: All’s Fair leans into the absurdity in its second season
content.shortHeadline: All’s Fair may be getting good at being ridiculous
content.standfirst: Ryan Murphy’s divorce-lawyer drama returns with scorpion-themed parties, implausible cases and Glenn Close in pleather. The Guardian still finds it ludicrous, but detects enough self-aware fun to award a star this time.

image.caption: Kim Kardashian, Naomi Watts and Sarah Paulson in All’s Fair.

sources.originalTitle: All’s Fair season two review – am I delirious … or is this getting good?

segments.body: The second season of All’s Fair picks up with the all-female divorce firm amid rivalries, a mysterious figure outside a house and a case involving an unsigned prenup and invisible ink. The Guardian’s review relishes the show’s outlandish details while remaining astonished by its dialogue and plotting.

segments.title: From bad to entertaining?
segments.body: The reviewer says the series is still ridiculous, but suggests it may be moving towards “so bad it’s good” territory. Kardashian’s character and the show’s camp flourishes offer occasional self-aware fun, even if the review remains far from convinced by the drama as a whole.

content.headline: The One About Matthew Perry raises questions its subject already answered
content.shortHeadline: Matthew Perry’s documentary adds little to his own account
content.standfirst: Netflix’s three-part documentary draws on archive and testimony from Perry’s loved ones, but the i Paper argues that his memoir already told much of this story. Its scenes of bereaved family members also raise questions about what the series adds.

image.caption: The One About Matthew Perry, a Netflix documentary series.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Matthew Perry documentary is undignified and intrusive

segments.body: The One About Matthew Perry traces the actor’s career, addiction and death at 54. The i Paper says archive footage and interviews with people close to him make for moving viewing, but much of the story was already told in Perry’s 2022 memoir. The documentary offers little new insight into the circumstances around his death or the wider exploitation of wealthy people struggling with addiction.

segments.title: The cost of access
segments.body: The review is troubled by the camera lingering on relatives as they recall learning of Perry’s death, and asks whether their distress serves the audience or the actor’s memory. It argues that his own words and performances remain a more respectful way to understand his life.

content.headline: What to watch this November: new dramas, comedies and a Blade Runner series
content.shortHeadline: November TV: The Greatest, Black Doves and more
content.standfirst: BBC Culture’s viewing guide ranges from a Muhammad Ali drama to new seasons of Black Doves and Stick, plus a Blade Runner spin-off. It offers a broad introduction to the month’s international television releases.

sources.originalTitle: The Greatest to Blade Runner 2099: 12 of the best TV shows to watch this November

segments.body: Among the month’s releases, The Greatest follows Muhammad Ali’s early life and boxing career, while Black Doves returns with Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw in an espionage story. Stick brings Owen Wilson back as a former golf champion, and the guide also points to the new series It Gets Worse and The Good Daughter.

segments.title: A science-fiction return
segments.body: The guide also includes Blade Runner 2099, starring Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer. It describes a future in which replicants pursue humans, shifting the franchise’s familiar premise and extending its questions about artificial intelligence and humanity.

content.headline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans grieving a lost future
content.shortHeadline: BioWare’s closure ends a chapter for Mass Effect fans
content.standfirst: EA has closed the studio behind Mass Effect and cancelled its next game, with more than 400 people losing their jobs. A former industry worker and long-time fan reflects on what the studio’s choice-driven stories meant to players.

image.caption: Mass Effect 3, part of BioWare’s Mass Effect series.

sources.originalTitle: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft

segments.body: The Guardian reports that EA has closed BioWare, a studio with a 30-year history, and cancelled its forthcoming Mass Effect game. The writer, who has spent 15 years in the games industry and nearly 20 as a fan, connects the closure to EA’s financial pressure and BioWare’s lack of a major critical or commercial success in more than a decade.

segments.title: The agency of playing
segments.body: The writer’s account centres on the original Mass Effect trilogy, whose characters and branching decisions made the story feel personal. Players could shape Commander Shepard and live with the consequences across three games. That sense of agency, the writer argues, helped make BioWare’s imagined future feel uniquely their own—and makes the cancelled sequel’s absence sting.

content.headline: Titanium Court makes a strange, unforgettable game out of fairies and songs
content.shortHeadline: Titanium Court is a game of delightful surprises
content.standfirst: This odd, pink 8-bit world mixes strategy, Shakespearean echoes and optional songs about salmon. The Guardian’s writer finds its pleasure in never knowing what the game will do next.

image.caption: A scene from Titanium Court.

sources.originalTitle: Why the weirdest game of 2026 is also one of my favourites

segments.body: Titanium Court begins as a strategy game in which players arrange battlefields for tiny fairy armies, but it soon becomes something stranger. In one encounter, a boss fight gives way to an optional musical performance and a long introduction about Pacific salmon. The Guardian calls the game a memorable collision of 8-bit visuals, Shakespearean ideas and unexpected songs.

segments.title: Letting the strangeness work
segments.body: Developer AP Thomson tells the Guardian that fairies gave him room to throw different ideas into the game, including music he developed at open-mic nights. The review recommends not explaining too much: discovering its strange logic and unpredictable scenes is part of the appeal. Its deliberately uncanny stock-photo-inspired look adds to the sense that the world never quite behaves as expected.

content.headline: Night Plane turns flight-attendant tasks into a trip to horror’s edge
content.shortHeadline: Night Plane makes a job simulator into horror
content.standfirst: This retro-style indie game begins with check-in and drinks service before a plane crash changes everything. The Guardian praises its uneasy blend of workplace routine, absurd humour and genuinely disturbing imagery.

image.caption: A scene from Night Plane.

sources.originalTitle: Night Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head trip

segments.body: In Night Plane, players start work as a flight attendant, checking tickets and serving passengers. After a crash, the routine begins again in an airport where some customers are demons disguised as people. The Guardian says the game uses familiar job-simulation tasks to build a sense of repetition and unease before bending them into horror.

segments.title: A strange and effective tone
segments.body: Low-polygon visuals recall the early PlayStation era, while flickering lights, strange dialogue and unsettling figures deepen the atmosphere. The review says a dry comic tone keeps the game from becoming predictable, even as its imagery grows genuinely disturbing. It also notes that later playthroughs reveal additional quests and endings.

content.headline: After 50 years playing games, a radio presenter finds himself in one
content.shortHeadline: A lifelong gamer steps into a video-game role
content.standfirst: Playing the lead character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake sent the Guardian writer to a rural Nova Scotia garage to record his lines. The experience changed how he thinks about voice acting—and gave his children a moment they will remember.

image.caption: Draga, the protagonist of Black Tides Draga’s Wake.

sources.originalTitle: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one

segments.body: After decades as a player, the Guardian writer was invited to voice Draga, a sailor in the survival-horror game Black Tides Draga’s Wake. He describes struggling at first to hear his own voice in the character, then learning to lower it and make the performance feel less forced. The most awkward task was recording improvised fight noises in a garage in rural Nova Scotia.

segments.title: From performance to family memory
segments.body: The project’s small, internationally scattered team reminded the writer of early home-computer game-making and its shared enthusiasm. Playing the finished game made him think about the characters’ lack of free will, but the experience also led to a favourite moment as a parent: showing his children the game without telling them he was in it, then watching them recognise his voice.

content.headline: The films that helped shape Grand Theft Auto’s cinematic worlds
content.shortHeadline: The films behind Grand Theft Auto’s movie-like worlds
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s games have borrowed from crime and action cinema for decades. The Guardian traces influences from Speed and Miami Vice to Boyz n the Hood, Heat and Bonnie and Clyde.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto 6.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s so glossy and sexy!’: 10 movies (and one TV show) that inspired Grand Theft Auto

segments.body: Grand Theft Auto has drawn on the visual language and stories of action and crime films to build its open worlds. The Guardian traces early inspiration from Speed and 1970s urban crime cinema through to Miami Vice, whose use of colour and night lighting helped inform Vice City.

segments.title: From gangster films to Los Santos
segments.body: The feature links Goodfellas and other Martin Scorsese films to GTA’s interest in crime, popular music and betrayal, and sees Boyz n the Hood in the setting and cultural references of San Andreas. Heat and Bonnie and Clyde offer further templates for heists and couples on the run—showing how the series has repeatedly turned film influences into playable worlds.

content.headline: Study warns plant-based dairy swaps could deepen iodine deficiencies
content.shortHeadline: Plant-based dairy swaps could deepen iodine gaps
content.standfirst: A UK modelling study found that replacing some dairy with unfortified alternatives could worsen shortfalls in iodine and other nutrients, particularly among teenage girls and women of childbearing age.

image.caption: Plant-based milk alternatives are often not fortified with iodine, researchers say.

sources.originalTitle: Swapping from dairy to plant-based milk, cheese and yoghurt ‘could lead to micronutrient deficiencies’

segments.body: Researchers modelled the effects of replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives using UK dietary data and products on sale. Replacing 20% to 30% of dairy intake could raise the share of teenage girls with inadequate iodine intake from 54% to 65%, and of women aged 19 to 49 from 32% to 42%.

segments.title: Fortification is uneven
segments.body: The study examined 289 plant-based milks, yoghurts and cheeses. While 61% contained added calcium and 46% vitamin B12, only 12% were fortified with iodine. The researchers found that standard iodine fortification of alternatives could prevent average declines; adding iodised salt to bread also reduced shortfalls in their model.

These are modelled dietary outcomes, not evidence that everyone switching to plant-based products will become deficient. A dietitian cited in the study said overall diet matters and advised checking labels for fortified options. The researchers also note that iodine is particularly important for growth and brain development.

content.headline: Scientists report possible red blood cell traces in a 115m-year-old dinosaur
content.shortHeadline: Possible blood-cell traces found in dinosaur bone
content.standfirst: Researchers say structures and chemical signals in an Aratasaurus fossil may preserve traces of blood biology. Another palaeontologist disputes the cell identification, and the findings do not suggest ancient DNA survives.

image.caption: Prof Kliti Grice with fossilised remains of the Aratasaurus.

sources.originalTitle: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists

segments.body: Researchers studying the hind leg bone of an Aratasaurus from what is now north-eastern Brazil found small structures resembling red blood cells in channels where blood vessels once ran. Chemical tests detected heme, a component involved in oxygen transport, along with traces of collagen’s amino acid building blocks.

segments.title: A contested interpretation
segments.body: The team suggests a manganese compound may have helped preserve the structures and molecules. But palaeontologist Mary Schweitzer is not convinced the shapes are red blood cells: she says they lack the dome-like nuclear bulge she would expect. She found the chemical evidence more persuasive, while the researchers stress that their claim is not evidence of preserved dinosaur DNA.

content.headline: US prosecutors drop charges against Harvard scientist detained over frog embryos
content.shortHeadline: US drops charges against detained Harvard scientist
content.standfirst: Kseniia Petrova spent four months in immigration detention after arriving with research samples. Prosecutors sought dismissal, citing office priorities and resources, while her lawyer says the unusual prosecution should never have been brought.

image.caption: Kseniia Petrova leaves a federal courthouse in Boston after her release on bail in June 2025.

sources.originalTitle: US prosecutors drop criminal charges against scientist detained over frog embryos

segments.body: Federal prosecutors have dropped all criminal charges against Kseniia Petrova, a Russian scientist at Harvard Medical School. She was arrested in March 2025 after returning from France with frog embryo samples for research and was charged with smuggling, concealing facts and making false statements.

segments.title: The case and its claims
segments.body: A judge dismissed the charges after prosecutors requested it, saying the costs of continuing outweighed the public interest in resolving the case. Petrova’s lawyers had argued the prosecution was vindictive and unusual. The Department of Homeland Security had maintained that she lied to federal officers about the samples; her lawyer described them as inert and non-toxic.

content.headline: Medical micro-robots move closer to targeted drug delivery
content.shortHeadline: Micro-robots aim to deliver drugs more precisely
content.standfirst: A small robot delivered insulin to a pig’s lower intestine in a reported test, while another device has been guided through a pig’s bloodstream. Both are experimental; wider medical use remains a distant prospect.

image.caption: Illustration of a small robot designed to deliver drugs to a precise location in the gut.

sources.originalTitle: The astonishing micro-robots you swallow that spot cancer and might help treat it

segments.body: Researchers in Beijing have developed a 6.5mm “spiny milli-ball robot” designed to carry drugs to a chosen point in the gut. In a test reported this month, it was steered into a pig’s lower intestine, where it delivered insulin. The device is swallowed in a capsule that dissolves in the stomach.

segments.title: Experiments beyond the gut
