segments.body: Other researchers have guided a 2mm robot through a pig’s bloodstream using magnets and X-ray imaging, and used a silicone model of the brain’s circulation to test delivery of a clot-dissolving drug. A separate group has shown magnetic particles heating and destroying tumours in mice. These are early research demonstrations, not established treatments for people.

content.headline: Could Verica have been a queen? Archaeologists dispute a new theory
content.shortHeadline: Was Verica a queen? Historians dispute the theory
content.standfirst: Archaeologist Miles Russell argues that the Iron Age ruler who sought Roman support may have been a woman. Coin evidence and Latin usage underpin his case, but other specialists say the evidence is inconclusive.

image.caption: Artist’s impression of Verica, whose sex is the subject of a disputed historical theory.

sources.originalTitle: Historians say King Verica persuaded Rome to invade Britain. But could Verica actually have been a queen?

segments.body: Miles Russell of Bournemouth University argues that Verica, ruler of the Atrebates, may have been a woman. He points to the name’s Latin ending, coins bearing the title “Rex” and imagery he reads as feminine. Russell says Verica’s appeal to Rome helped set the stage for Claudius’s invasion of Britain in AD43.

segments.title: Evidence under debate
segments.body: Oxford archaeologist Roger Tomlin says the masculine form “Vericus” supports a feminine reading of Verica, but questions whether “Rex” was used for rulers of either sex. Coin expert Daphne Nash Briggs also disputes Russell’s reading, citing coins that she says depict male figures. The interpretation remains contested.

content.headline: NASA’s X-70 Fractal will test next-generation aircraft technology
content.shortHeadline: NASA plans crewed X-70 research aircraft
content.standfirst: NASA says its new X-plane is designed as a reconfigurable test platform for flight-control and manoeuvrability research, with a first flight under the agency expected within two years.

sources.originalTitle: The X-70 is NASA’s next experimental X-plane

segments.body: NASA has announced the X-70 Fractal, a crewed experimental aircraft intended to test aviation technologies in flight. The agency says it will cruise at Mach 0.75, reach altitudes up to 45,000 feet and carry as much as 2,000 pounds of experimental equipment. NASA expects its first flight under the agency within two years.

The aircraft is designed to let NASA rapidly reconfigure flight controls and swap equipment between experiments. The agency has released an AI-generated image rather than a photograph of the aircraft; the supplied reporting does not provide further design details.

content.headline: MPs warn UK remains dangerously dependent on China for critical minerals
content.shortHeadline: UK warned of dangerous reliance on China for minerals
content.standfirst: A parliamentary committee says dependence on Chinese supplies and processing threatens defence, AI and net-zero plans. The government says it is funding domestic production and recycling and has set targets for 2035.

image.caption: Rare earths and other critical minerals are used in defence and technology products.

sources.originalTitle: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI

segments.body: A House of Commons business committee says the UK is dangerously reliant on China for critical minerals used in defence, renewable energy and AI. It identifies mineral processing as a particular bottleneck, with China dominant in refining several materials, including lithium and rare earths.

segments.title: A proposed response
segments.body: The committee called for a centralised policy, financing for mines and other projects, and closer work with G7 partners and other suppliers. It cited estimates that demand for lithium could rise 45-fold by 2030 and demand for rare earths 16-fold. The government says it is providing £400m for domestic production and recycling, with goals for 2035.

content.headline: UK considers restricting sales of smart glasses amid covert filming fears
content.shortHeadline: UK considers smart-glasses sales restrictions
content.standfirst: A minister says the government is exploring limits on sales to certain users and use in some settings, amid reports of people being filmed without consent. The devices can also help some people with visual impairment.

image.caption: Smart glasses with built-in cameras have prompted concerns about covert filming.

sources.originalTitle: UK government considers smart glasses ban over secret filming concerns

segments.body: The UK government is considering restrictions on smart glasses, including limiting sales to “certain users”, safeguarding minister Satvir Kaur told MPs. Her comments followed concerns that people have been filmed without their knowledge or consent using glasses with built-in cameras.

segments.title: Benefits and safeguards
segments.body: Kaur said the government is looking at restrictions in certain settings, while NHS England and the Department for Education are examining wearable technology in their sectors. She also noted that smart glasses can help visually impaired people navigate. Filming in some places, including courts, may already break the law.

content.headline: Zipline raises $1.5bn as Walmart plans 300 more drone-delivery sites
content.shortHeadline: Zipline raises $1.5bn for drone-delivery expansion
content.standfirst: The company says its new multi-year Walmart agreement will add 300 US delivery sites, far more than the 21 the partners currently operate. The expansion depends on scaling a business that is still growing.

image.caption: Zipline operates autonomous drones for deliveries.

sources.originalTitle: Zipline hits $21.5B valuation as Walmart expands bet on drone delivery

segments.body: Autonomous drone-delivery company Zipline has raised $1.5bn, valuing it at $21.5bn, and agreed with Walmart to add 300 delivery sites across the US. The companies currently have 21 active sites together. Zipline says it will use the funding to expand US manufacturing and hire workers.

segments.title: A business still scaling
segments.body: Zipline operates in five African countries, several US cities and Japan, delivering health, food, retail and agricultural products. Its smaller home-delivery drones are designed to carry up to eight pounds within a 10-mile radius; larger aircraft are used for longer routes. The company says its share of delivery revenue rose from 10.8% to 34.9% between March and October.

content.headline: Instagram brings its Edits video editor to Mac, adding agent tools
content.shortHeadline: Instagram brings Edits video editor to Mac
content.standfirst: The desktop app adds a multi-track timeline, 4K exports and the option to connect AI agents for rough cuts. It is currently limited to macOS, with cross-device project editing still in development.

sources.originalTitle: Instagram brings Edits to desktop to take on CapCut
You can edit your videos with AI on Instagram’s new desktop Edits app

segments.body: Instagram has brought its Edits video editor to Mac, positioning it more directly against ByteDance’s CapCut. The app includes a multi-track timeline, keyframes, audio waveforms, automatic captions and watermark-free 4K exports, and lets creators publish directly to Instagram.

segments.title: Agents and current limits
segments.body: Instagram says users can connect an AI agent through an interface to create a rough cut, then continue editing manually. The Verge’s reporting also describes this agent integration. The desktop app is currently for macOS only; Instagram says it is working on editing a single project across mobile and desktop.

content.headline: Data-centre opposition gains political and public momentum
content.shortHeadline: Data-centre opposition grows across Europe and the US
content.standfirst: Campaigners across 15 European countries are calling for a halt to large projects, while US election results have strengthened opponents of rapid expansion. A proposed Norwich site shows how local environmental and energy concerns are playing out.

image.caption: A protest at a data-centre development near West Kilbride, Scotland.

sources.originalTitle: Activists across Europe prepare two days of protests against datacentres
After the midterms, a bigger clash over data centers could be coming
Developer says £1.2bn data centre will boost city
Tech is about to get hammered in Congress

segments.body: More than 100 groups are organising protests in 15 European countries, seeking a moratorium on large data centres over environmental and social costs. In the US, opposition to data-centre projects featured in midterm campaigns, and a county in Ohio voted to ban planned development, according to the reporting.

segments.title: Local stakes, wider debate
segments.body: In Norfolk, a developer has proposed a £1.2bn data centre near Norwich that would need 150MW of power. The developer says it could benefit the region and that its assessments predict no discernible impact on nearby nature reserves; campaigners have raised concerns about the site’s proximity to protected habitat. A decision is expected early next year.

perspectives.body: Norwich Apex chief executive Matt Bartram says the project could help make Norwich a “tech hub”. He says its closed-loop cooling system would need no additional water once filled and that measures would limit noise.

segments.title: Possible policy consequences
segments.body: US lawmakers have proposed measures ranging from local construction pauses to requiring data centres to pay for grid upgrades. Organisers of the European protests also cite emissions and pressure on energy and land. The reporting describes opposition and proposals, not a settled change in policy across either region.

content.headline: Big Tech plans more AI spending as returns remain uncertain
content.shortHeadline: AI buildout spending surges, but returns remain unclear
content.standfirst: Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta plan at least $720bn in capital spending this year, much of it for AI infrastructure. Their growing revenues have yet to settle investors’ doubts about the costs and eventual returns.

sources.originalTitle: Big Tech’s big AI buildout will not end until someone stops it

segments.body: Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta plan to spend at least $720bn on capital investment this year, much of it on AI infrastructure, according to the reporting. They have also arranged at least $1tn in spending commitments for later years, even as investors question when the buildout will pay off.

segments.title: Costs outpace some returns
segments.body: The report notes strong revenue growth at several companies, but says it may not justify the scale of investment. Google executives acknowledged that AI Mode queries bring lower monetisation than traditional search, while Anthropic reported $17bn in quarterly revenue and $17.5bn in computing costs. These figures do not establish whether the investment will ultimately be profitable.

content.headline: AI agents formally verify a major mathematics library, startup says
content.shortHeadline: AI agents verify a major mathematics library
content.standfirst: Axiom Math says its agents converted the Stacks Project into computer-checked Lean code, a large formalisation effort in algebraic geometry. The result is a verification milestone, not proof that AI can independently advance mathematics.

image.caption: Axiom Math, the company that says its agents formally verified the Stacks Project.

sources.originalTitle: Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics

segments.body: Axiom Math says its agents have formally verified the Stacks Project, an open-source mathematics library spanning algebra, geometry and number theory. The company reports translating roughly 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of Lean code, which a proof assistant checks line by line.

segments.title: Why formalisation matters
segments.body: Formal verification checks whether each proof follows its stated logic and whether its links to earlier definitions and results remain intact. Axiom says the work adds a reusable base for algebraic geometry, an area it describes as poorly represented in formalised mathematics. The report does not establish that the system can discover new results autonomously.

content.headline: Startup offers $1m for AI solutions to open materials-science problems
content.shortHeadline: Startup offers $1m for AI materials-science challenges
content.standfirst: Discovered Materials is offering five prizes to set measurable tests for AI progress in materials science. Models the company tested did not make much headway, and the challenges remain open.

image.caption: Discovered Materials, the startup behind the materials-science challenge.

sources.originalTitle: A YC startup is putting $1M behind five unsolved materials science problems for AI

segments.body: Discovered Materials has announced five open materials-science problems, with a total prize pool of $1m for solutions. The startup says the questions were defined with academic advisers to make progress easier to assess in a field where problems are harder to frame as a simple right-or-wrong test than in mathematics.

The company says AI agents it tried on the problems worked for several days without making much headway. The challenges are intended as goalposts for measuring progress, not evidence that current systems can solve them. The startup’s main business is using AI to search for materials for semiconductors.

content.headline: Agility Robotics goes public as questions remain over humanoid robots
content.shortHeadline: Agility Robotics goes public with humanoid robot plans
content.standfirst: The company is raising $465m through a reverse merger as it pitches its Digit robots for repetitive industrial work. It has customer contracts in prospect, but its revenue remains small beside its reported losses.

image.caption: Agility Robotics’ Digit robot is designed for repetitive industrial work.

sources.originalTitle: Agility is the first pure humanoid robot company on the stock market. Are you buying?

segments.body: Agility Robotics is going public through a reverse merger that is expected to raise $465m. The company says nine industrial customers have used its Digit robots, including for moving heavy totes. It reported $174,000 in revenue for the first half of 2026 and a $362m loss over the same period.

segments.title: The commercial test ahead
segments.body: Agility says it has $300m in planned contracts for its next-generation Digit 5, but customers must first meet undisclosed performance targets. The company has not yet shown the new model and says it will demonstrate it at CES 2027. Its robots can move and place loads, but complex manipulation remains a challenge across the field.

The company argues that robots can reduce costs for industrial customers, but whether the economics work depends on reliability, task accuracy, maintenance and the pace of new deployments. Agility’s chief executive says the company is focusing on repetitive manual work rather than spectacle; the business case remains to be demonstrated at scale.

content.headline: Liverpool lose 3-2 at Fenerbahce after twice taking the lead
content.shortHeadline: Liverpool surrender lead in 3-2 loss at Fenerbahce
content.standfirst: Liverpool’s first Champions League defeat by Fenerbahce came after they led twice, including through Alexander Isak’s 69th-minute header. Andoni Iraola called the goals conceded “cheap” and “messy”.

image.caption: Liverpool suffered their first Champions League defeat by Fenerbahce.

sources.originalTitle: Another 'miracle' in Istanbul - but this one hurt Liverpool

segments.body: Liverpool were beaten 3-2 in Istanbul after taking the lead twice. Trey Nyoni opened the scoring, and Alexander Isak put them ahead again in the 69th minute, but Fenerbahce struck three times from set-pieces to complete the comeback.

segments.title: A familiar defensive concern
segments.body: Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock said the defeat exposed recurring problems: mistakes at set-pieces and balls into the box, and a team that can look vulnerable on the counter-attack. He said Liverpool’s inability to see out a game after going ahead was frustrating for supporters.

content.headline: LIV Golf set to wind down after replacement funding falls through
content.shortHeadline: LIV Golf faces wind-down as replacement funding falls through
content.standfirst: The financing firm that had considered backing a new version of LIV Golf has decided a deal is not viable. An attorney is expected to tell a court on Thursday that the LIV 2.0 proposal cannot proceed.

sources.originalTitle: LIV to wind down after backers withdraw support

segments.body: LIV Golf is set to be wound down after BC Partners Credit withdrew from a possible financing deal, BBC Sport reports. The firm had considered providing about $300m for LIV 2.0, after Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund withdrew its backing in April.

segments.title: A proposed revival stalled
segments.body: Sources told BBC Sport that the LIV 2.0 team had commitments from co-investors and about 30 players, including major winners, but could not secure the agreements needed in time. The expected court announcement would mark a major turn in a saga that has unsettled the golf calendar and left players’ futures uncertain.

content.headline: Tenerife mourns De Miguel as goalkeeper Owono speaks of his grief
content.shortHeadline: Tenerife mourns De Miguel; Owono speaks of his grief
content.standfirst: Tributes have gathered at Tenerife’s stadium after striker Jesus de Miguel died from injuries sustained in a collision during Monday’s match. FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is struggling to come to terms with the loss.

image.caption: Fans gather to pay their respects to Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel.

sources.originalTitle: An island in mourning: Tenerife processes death of De Miguel
'Most difficult days of my life' for keeper Owono

segments.body: Fans have laid flowers, scarves, photographs and children’s drawings outside Tenerife’s stadium, where hundreds have gathered to pay their respects. De Miguel, 30, died after a collision with Owono during a match on Monday. Tenerife said six official days of mourning would begin.

segments.title: Owono’s statement
segments.body: Owono said through his club that these were “the most difficult days of my life” and that he could think only of De Miguel and the pain felt by those who loved him. Police have opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter; the inquiry is ongoing.

perspectives.body: Owono said he would face whatever issues arose with respect, but that his thoughts were with De Miguel, his family and everyone who loved him. His club also said team-mate Lautaro Spatz described the goalkeeper as devastated and said he would never intentionally hurt anyone.

content.headline: Djokovic’s ATP Finals hopes end as Zverev questions scrutiny of his ranking
content.shortHeadline: Djokovic out of ATP Finals race; Zverev questions scrutiny
content.standfirst: Novak Djokovic lost to qualifier Rinky Hijikata in Paris and can no longer qualify for the ATP Finals. Alexander Zverev, also beaten at the Masters, said he was annoyed at having to justify becoming world number one.

sources.originalTitle: Defeat ends Djokovic's hopes of making ATP Finals
Zverev annoyed by reaction to becoming world number one

segments.body: Djokovic’s 2-6 6-3 6-3 defeat by world number 83 Hijikata ended his bid to reach the ATP Finals in Turin. He was likely to need a semi-final run in Paris to qualify. Djokovic said his plan for the coming weeks was “just rest” after a season in which he failed to reach the quarter-finals at any Masters 1000 event.

segments.title: Zverev objects to the reaction
segments.body: Zverev lost his first match since becoming world number one, going down 7-6 (7-5) 6-2 to Lorenzo Musetti. He said it was “annoying” that he felt he had to explain why it was acceptable for him to hold the ranking, while acknowledging he had played badly against Musetti.

content.headline: Brazilian under-20 match sees record 51 red cards after brawl
content.shortHeadline: Record 51 red cards shown after Brazilian youth-game brawl
content.standfirst: The abandoned Minas Gerais Under-20 Championship semi-final between Uberlandia and Mamore produced 51 dismissals: 43 players and eight members of staff. Uberlandia later conceded the second leg, saying Mamore had only seven players available.

image.caption: Players and staff were sent off after a brawl during the under-20 match.

sources.originalTitle: World record 51 red cards shown in Brazilian youth game

segments.body: A brawl during the second half led to 43 players and eight coaching staff being sent off, a reported world record. The game was paused for about 40 minutes before the referee abandoned it. Police were called after damage was reported at the stadium.

segments.title: The tie’s outcome
segments.body: Uberlandia confirmed they had conceded the semi-final’s second leg because Mamore had only seven players available after the dismissals. The club called the decision a “gesture of fair play”; Mamore will progress to the final.

content.headline: Sweeney says England must improve discipline before Australia opener
content.shortHeadline: Sweeney urges England to cut cards before Australia opener
content.standfirst: RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney says England are the world’s second-best side when they keep 15 players on the pitch, but fall well down the rankings when reduced to 14. England begin their November campaign against Australia on Sunday.

image.caption: England players Henry Pollock and Freddie Steward were shown yellow cards against Ireland.

sources.originalTitle: Sweeney demands discipline from card-happy England

segments.body: England received eight yellow cards and one red across their five Six Nations matches, and spent 118 minutes with fewer than 15 players. Sweeney said the team’s discipline had been the subject of internal discussion and that head coach Steve Borthwick was working with players to address it.

segments.title: A new tournament’s first finals weekend
segments.body: England face Australia on Sunday, followed by Japan and New Zealand, before the Nations Championship finals weekend. Sweeney said ticket sales for the new event’s Friday fixtures had been challenging, adding that some fans did not yet fully understand the format.

content.headline: Finn Russell targets historic Scotland win over New Zealand
content.shortHeadline: Russell eyes historic Scotland win over New Zealand
content.standfirst: Scotland host the All Blacks on Saturday, seeking a first win over New Zealand in 121 years. Finn Russell says he feels fresher this season and that Scotland must turn belief into results.

image.caption: Finn Russell prepares for Scotland’s Nations Championship match against New Zealand.

sources.originalTitle: No end in sight for Russell as he eyes famous All Blacks win
Scottish Rugby

segments.body: Russell, preparing for his 96th Scotland cap, says he feels good mentally and physically after finding the season following the Lions tour demanding in the past. He says Scotland need to improve how they convert opportunities in the opposition’s 22 if they are to take the next step.

segments.title: A formidable test
segments.body: Scotland have come close to beating New Zealand in recent meetings but have not ended a 121-year wait for a win. Assistant coach Pete Horne said the All Blacks had regained some of their old aura under Dave Rennie; lock Scott Cummings said Scotland had learned from past games about managing momentum.

content.headline: Everton compensation masks Burnley’s £47.8m underlying loss
content.shortHeadline: Everton payout masks Burnley’s £47.8m underlying loss
content.standfirst: Burnley reported a £9m loss for 2025-26, but without a disputed £38.8m payment from Everton the loss would have been £47.8m. An appeal over the compensation is expected to be heard in January.

image.caption: Burnley’s takeover used loans secured against club assets and other external debt.

sources.originalTitle: How landmark Everton compensation prevented Burnley record loss

segments.body: The £38.8m compensation, linked to Everton’s profit and sustainability breach and its effect on Burnley’s relegation prospects, helped make the latest accounts look healthier. The award is subject to appeal, and Burnley’s board says the outcome cannot be reasonably determined.

segments.title: Debt and repayment risks remain
segments.body: Burnley’s reported debt fell to £62.9m, but the club still faces significant repayments and is negotiating to refinance its facilities. Football finance professor Kieran Maguire said the underlying issues remained, noting the club was still losing more than £1m a week despite Premier League revenues.
